source.title: Scaling Fine-Grained MoE Beyond 50B Parameters: Empirical Evaluation and Practical Insights
source.authors: Jakub Krajewski; Marcin Chochowski; Daniel Korzekwa

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation loss and downstream benchmark outcomes across matched MoE configurations, testing architecture sensitivity and whether loss improvements accompany downstream improvements. It does not fit or test the general power laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study varies MoE granularity, training duration, model size, and router normalization order, and reports validation losses and downstream results. It does not fit scaling-law curves, test extrapolation from small runs, or search for compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Cited results from other papers and router-logit/load-balance measurements are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares MoE language models matched in total and active parameters, which bears loosely on V4 (architecture detail at fixed size) and on V6 (whether downstream scores track pretraining loss). It fits no power laws, makes no extrapolation and searches no compute-optimal split. Its setting (MoE granularity and router design) is new relative to the dense-model originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that fine-grained MoE gives lower validation loss and better downstream scores than matched standard MoE, with benefits growing with training length and scale. They add that at 11B/50B tokens granularity gives no significant gain for the Mixtral-style model, and that applying softmax after Top-k is markedly better for fine-grained MoE.
record.recipe_differences: This is an empirical comparison of MoE granularity and router design, not a reproduction of the original dense-language-model scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Granularity gains vary with training duration, model size, and MoE routing variant. Router softmax/Top-k ordering changes validation loss, with the paper reporting a larger effect for fine-grained than standard MoE.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The validation-loss curves at the 25B and 100B token horizons are shown only in a figure without tabulated values. The study's comparisons do not fit general scaling laws or isolate downstream predictability across model sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining individual benchmark cells from Tables 2 and 5 were not extracted: the tables report more per-task cells than the 60-row limit allows. The retained rows prioritize the aggregate averages, task-level reversals, and representative 56B task outcomes. All reported validation-loss table entries and Table 6 router-order results were retained.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
Depth, width, aspect ratio and attention-head choices are not varied. Only MoE granularity at G=1 vs 8 and softmax/Top-k order are tested, at two sizes.
Only text-and-code LM pretraining; no other modalities or regimes.
No fitted mapping from loss or scale to downstream scores. Benchmark models also received extra continued pretraining after the loss measurements.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Training-step savings relative to 1xFLOPs-G1 at 25B/50B/100B tokens: 1xG8 21.6/27.9/33.6%, 2xG1 34.5/32.8/32.8%, 2xG8 24.6/32.8/39.4%
Remaining per-benchmark cells, e.g. CommonsenseQA and SocialIQA at 56B, and the 11B 1xFLOPs pair tasks

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The V4 link is loose: MoE granularity is an architecture detail at fixed total and active parameters, not dense depth/width. Many rows are duplicate pairs (main and comparator). The reader marked comparator rows reversed by mistake; for V6 the relevant question is whether the score ordering follows the loss ordering. There are no uncertainty estimates and only a single seed per configuration.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or tests of loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
No prediction of larger-run losses from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute search or fitted trends for optimal parameter and token counts.
Tests MoE granularity and router softmax/Top-k order, not depth, width, or a broad range of other architecture details.
Only text-and-code language-model pretraining is studied; no other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Compares validation loss and downstream results across MoE variants; does not fit a predictive mapping or establish downstream scaling across model sizes.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted and compared across setup or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: MoE models at fixed total and active parameters (11B/50B tokens and 56B/300B tokens), varying expert granularity and router softmax/Top-k order
relationships.reason: Granularity shifts validation loss by 0.002 to 0.05 (at most about 2.2%) and router order by 0.007 to 0.036, both small effects (r1-r8, r53-r58).
relationships.display_finding: Expert granularity changed validation loss by 0.002–0.05, at most about 2.2%, while router ordering changed it by 0.007–0.036.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: MoE models at fixed total and active parameters (11B/50B tokens and 56B/300B tokens), varying expert granularity and router softmax/Top-k order
source_check.reason: Tables 2 and 5 confirm granularity loss differences of 0.002–0.050; Table 6 confirms router-order differences of 0.007–0.036. These are modest loss changes in the tested settings.

relationships.condition: Effect of granularity across training horizons for 11B models (25B/50B/100B tokens)
relationships.reason: The granularity effect on loss grows with training length, and the small loss gaps equal 22-39% training-step savings (Table 3, text-based; r49-r52 are figure-only). So 'little' depends on horizon and on the metric used.
relationships.display_finding: Granularity affected loss more strongly with longer training, and the small loss differences corresponded to 22–39% fewer training steps.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Effect of granularity across training horizons for 11B models (25B/50B/100B tokens)
source_check.reason: Section 3.3 explicitly reports increasing granularity benefits with training duration. Table 3 gives fine-grained-model step savings of 21.6–39.4%, all relative to standard Switch 1xFLOPs-G1; these qualify the practical meaning of small loss differences.

relationships.condition: Benchmark averages for matched pairs at 11B and 56B
relationships.reason: In all four pairs the lower-loss variant has the higher benchmark average, and the 56B cross-pair near-tie in loss gives near-equal averages (r9, r10, r13-r16).
relationships.display_finding: The lower-loss variant achieved the higher benchmark average in all four matched pairs, while nearly equal losses at 56B accompanied nearly equal averages.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Benchmark averages for matched pairs at 11B and 56B
source_check.reason: Tables 2 and 5 show higher averages for the lower-loss member of all four matched pairs. At 56B, losses 1.779 and 1.780 accompany averages 59.0 and 58.8. This supports qualitative tracking, without establishing a quantitative prediction law.

relationships.condition: Individual benchmarks, and the 11B Mixtral-style pair with near-identical loss
relationships.reason: The averages differ by 1 point at a 0.002 loss gap, and several tasks rank the higher-loss model better: PIQA, WinoGrande, OpenbookQA, RACE (r11, r12, r17-r24).
relationships.display_finding: Average scores differed by one point despite a 0.002 loss gap, and PIQA, WinoGrande, OpenbookQA and RACE favored the higher-loss model.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Individual benchmarks, and the 11B Mixtral-style pair with near-identical loss

source_check.notes: Table 3 savings use 1xFLOPs-G1 as the common baseline, not each variant's matched-granularity counterpart; hardware utilization is assumed equal. Resource matching excludes routers, Switch granularity comparisons also change router order, and benchmark models receive additional continued pretraining equal to 10% of the original token budget.
